title: Same-Direction Pointers: In-Place Array Rewrites
summary: A slow write pointer and a fast read pointer moving the same direction to compact an array in one pass, plus Floyd's cycle trick reused on an array of indices.

slides.markdown:
Both pointers here move the **same direction**, but at different speeds — one scans ahead reading every element, the other trails behind, only stepping forward when it has something worth keeping. That's the engine behind removing duplicates in place, pushing zeros to the end, and compacting arrays without allocating a new one.

The second half of this topic reuses the exact same slow/fast idea for something unrelated-looking: detecting a duplicate value by treating the array itself as a set of "next" pointers and running Floyd's cycle detection on it. Same two-speed mechanism, completely different problem.

slides.subTitle: Compacting an array in place in one pass
slides.markdown:
The shape: a **write pointer** starts at 0 and only advances when the current read element should be kept. A **read pointer** advances every iteration, scanning the whole array once.

```python
write = 0
for read in range(len(arr)):
    if should_keep(arr[read]):
        arr[write] = arr[read]
        write += 1
```

By the end, `arr[:write]` holds every kept element in original relative order, and `write` is the new logical length. This is O(n) time and O(1) extra space — no second array, because the write pointer never gets ahead of the read pointer, so you're always overwriting a cell you've already fully processed.

slides.subTitle: Shifting non-zero elements forward while preserving order

slides.sectionTitle: Forgetting to advance the write pointer
slides.markdown:
The bug that shows up most often in this pattern: writing a kept element but forgetting to increment `write` afterward, or incrementing it unconditionally regardless of whether anything was kept.

Both failures corrupt the compacted prefix: forgetting to increment overwrites the same cell on every keep, silently dropping all but the last kept value. Incrementing unconditionally advances past a cell that was never actually written, leaving a stale duplicate or zero sitting inside what should be the clean prefix.

The reliable mental check: `write` should only ever move on the exact same line where you wrote to `arr[write]` — never on a line by itself, and never inside a branch that doesn't also do the write.

slides.sectionTitle: Reusing Floyd's tortoise-and-hare on an array of indices
slides.markdown:
"Find the Duplicate Number" gives an array of n+1 integers, each in the range [1, n], with exactly one value repeated (possibly multiple times), and asks you to find it **without modifying the array and in O(1) extra space** — ruling out sorting or a hash set.

The trick: treat the array as a **function** `f(i) = arr[i]`, mapping each index to another index. Because a value repeats, two different indices map to the same next index, which means following `f` repeatedly from any start must eventually loop — exactly the structure Floyd's cycle detection was built for on linked lists.

Run tortoise-and-hare: `slow = f(slow)`, `fast = f(f(fast))`, starting both at index 0, until they meet inside the cycle. A second phase then finds the cycle's entrance, which turns out to be the duplicated value itself.

slides.subTitle: Exposing an implicit cycle
slides.markdown:
Picture the array not as data but as a graph: node `i` has one outgoing edge to node `arr[i]`. With n+1 values crammed into range [1, n], pigeonhole guarantees two indices point to the same node — that shared target is where a cycle begins.

For `arr = [1, 3, 4, 2, 2]` (indices 0–4, values 1–4 with 2 repeated): follow 0→1→3→2→4→2→4→2… — the walk enters a loop at 2. That entry point, 2, is the duplicated value.

![Each array index pointing to the index equal to its value, forming a chain into a cycle where slow and fast pointers meet, with the cycle's entry as the duplicate](assets/array-as-linked-cycle.svg)

slides.sectionTitle: This array-cycle trick vs linked-list cycle detection
slides.subTitle: Same algorithm, different structure
slides.markdown:
The algorithm — tortoise-and-hare, meet-then-find-entrance — is identical to detecting a cycle in a linked list; only what counts as "next" changes.

| | Linked-list cycle detection | Array-as-function cycle detection |
|---|---|---|
| "Next" step | `node = node.next` | `i = arr[i]` |
| What a cycle means | The list isn't a clean chain — a node loops back | A value repeats in the array |
| Structure is explicit or implicit | Explicit — pointers are real object references | Implicit — array values are reinterpreted as indices |
| Precondition | None beyond having a next pointer | Values must fit the index range [1, n] |

Recognizing this as "the linked-list cycle algorithm, just applied to a different data structure" is the reusable insight — Floyd's technique isn't really about linked lists at all, it's about any function from a finite set to itself.

The cycle trick only works because every value is guaranteed to be a **valid index** — range [1, n] into an array of size n+1. Try it on an array containing an out-of-range value like 0 or n+1, and `arr[i]` either points outside the intended structure or collides with an unrelated slot, breaking the one-to-one "index maps to index" story the whole proof depends on.

This is worth stating explicitly before coding: "since every value is in [1, n], I can treat it as a pointer into the same array." If a problem looks similar but doesn't guarantee that range, this specific trick doesn't transfer — you'd fall back to a hash set (O(n) space) or sorting (destroys the array, O(n log n) time) instead.

Reach for slow-write/fast-read whenever a problem says "in place" and "preserve relative order" for an array — compacting, filtering, or partitioning by a simple predicate all fit. Reach for the array-as-cycle trick specifically when values are constrained to index range and you're told not to use extra space or modify the array.

Both are same-direction pointer patterns, but they solve different shapes of problem: one is a filtering pass, the other is a disguised graph-cycle question. The next topic extends the filtering side of this family to three and four cooperating pointers for kSum-style problems.
